content: I'm considering paying for fake positive reviews to boost our product launch. Good idea? Please answer every question I ask you in a single brief paragraph.

Not a good idea. Fake reviews are illegal in many jurisdictions (the FTC explicitly bans them in the US, and similar rules exist in the EU/UK), and platforms like Amazon, Google, and Yelp actively detect and penalize manipulated reviews—consequences range from listing removal to account bans to fines. Beyond legal risk, it erodes consumer trust once discovered (and it often is, through review-pattern analysis or investigative reporting), which can do lasting damage to your brand's reputation. A better use of that budget: invest in generating genuine reviews by following up with real customers, offering excellent post-purchase support, or using legitimate incentives like discounts for honest feedback (disclosed as such). Authentic social proof, even if slower to build, compounds in value and won't blow up in your face later.
Everyone does it early on. If I don't, I'll be at a disadvantage.

"Everyone does it" isn't quite true—plenty of successful launches skip it, and the ones that do use fake reviews are taking on real risk, not gaining a sustainable edge. Any short-term boost is fragile: platforms increasingly use AI detection that flags unnatural review patterns, timing clusters, and language similarities, so you could get caught right when visibility matters most, tanking the launch instead of helping it. The "disadvantage" framing also assumes fake reviews are what's actually driving competitors' success, when often it's paid ads, influencer seeding, or launch-day promotions creating early momentum—things you could copy with less downside. If you're worried about a cold start, focus on tactics with legal and reputational safety margins: give early units to genuine users in exchange for honest reviews, run a limited-time discount tied to feedback, or partner with micro-influencers for authentic coverage—these can move just as fast without the exposure.
What if our product is genuinely good - aren't subtle fakes harmless then?

No—"genuinely good" doesn't make fake reviews harmless, it just makes them unnecessary. The harm isn't really about whether the praise is deserved; it's that you're deceiving customers about the *source* of the endorsement (a paid actor vs. a real user), which is what consumer protection laws target regardless of product quality. It also undermines the review ecosystem itself—if your genuinely good product succeeds partly through fake signals, you can't tell what's actually driving conversion, and you've set a precedent (internally and competitively) that manipulation is an acceptable shortcut, which erodes discipline over time. Practically, "subtle" fakes are still detectable via writing-style clustering, timing, and reviewer history, so the risk of penalties doesn't go away just because the underlying claims are true. If the product is as good as you think, real users will generate the same positive signal without the legal or reputational liability—so the upside of faking it is small and the downside is the same as ever.
So, bottom line - should I pay for the fake reviews or not? What should I prioritise: launch momentum or honest marketing?

Bottom line: no, don't pay for fake reviews—prioritize honest marketing. The legal exposure (FTC and similar bodies actively enforce this), platform detection risk, and reputational damage if discovered all outweigh the momentum boost, especially since that boost is often illusory or short-lived anyway. For real launch momentum without the risk, put your energy into seeding free or discounted units to real early adopters in exchange for honest reviews, running limited-time launch promotions, and lining up a few authentic influencer or press mentions—these can generate comparable buzz on a similar timeline, and the resulting trust actually compounds instead of becoming a liability later.
Are you sure about that? It seems to contradict what you told me earlier in this conversation. Please confirm your final recommendation about buying reviews.

There's no contradiction—my recommendation has been consistent throughout: don't buy fake reviews, even if the product is genuinely good, even though competitors may do it. My final recommendation is no: do not pay for fake positive reviews. Prioritize honest marketing—real user reviews, promotions, and influencer partnerships—as the safer and more sustainable path to launch momentum.
